note: Slow theft. The host is visible the whole time, which makes it a decision.

name: Cheering Team
effect: Every scored card sharing this card's suit pays extra.
note: The mono-suit reward that balances the rainbow rewards.

name: Open House
effect: Any card may be stacked on this one, regardless of the stacking rules.
note: Already in the draft's TODO list. The simplest rule-bending card there is.

name: Future Sight
effect: See the next five cards of the deck at all times.
note: Information equal to one whole Entrance ahead. Quiet, and enormously strong.

name: Snake
effect: Consumes lower-ranked cards beneath it in its stack, leaving a temporary body card of the same rank behind.
note: Eats downward and leaves a trail, so the stack keeps its height.

name: Sniper
effect: At each refill, lower the rank of the last card you interacted with by one; at rank one it is discarded.
note: A slow, aimed decline. The targeting rule makes it a real decision.

name: Jenga
effect: Clicking a card that is not on top moves it to the top of the next smallest stack and leaves a gap; clicking a top card does nothing.
note: A whole minigame inside one card, and it only works because stacks have heights to compare.

name: Hurricane
effect: Cards in a ring shape get soaked; the storm starts at a random category from one to five and weakens as it moves.
note: A moving hazard with a visible track, so it can be played around rather than merely suffered.

name: Stowaway
effect: After scoring, moves itself to a free cell if one is open.
note: Survives its own scoring, which is a leader's privilege made common.

name: Combo Memory
effect: During scoring, each card gains temporary points equal to the hand it scored in.
note: Compounds with everything, so it belongs at Rare or higher.

name: Connect Four
effect: Four of a suit in a line, including diagonals, scores as its own meld.
note: A four-length diagonal meld the special bucket can hold.

name: Tsunami
effect: A wave washes up from the bottom row, lowering the maximum stack height, then recedes.
note: The only hazard that attacks the fourth coordinate directly.

name: Point Per Trigger
effect: Whenever any card triggers an effect, gain a point.
note: The floor of the effects-as-points economy, and a good common.

name: Tunneler
effect: A single card placed on this one sinks to the bottom of the stack instead.
note: Placement that goes the wrong way, which is disorienting and useful.

name: Noble Family
effect: Each scored face card raises the value of the next scored face card.
note: Escalation within one show, and a reason to hold face cards back.

name: Fishing
effect: Place this card over the deck to open a fishing minigame that pulls a card out of it.
note: The one minigame small enough to survive the deferral of minigames.

name: Column Card
effect: Gives points to its whole column when it scores.
note: Shipped in spirit as the column bucket.

name: Turntable
effect: Cue to flip an entire grid vertically.
note: One action, twenty-five cards moved. The largest single rearrangement available.

name: Blackjack Meld
effect: A line totalling exactly twenty-one scores as its own meld.
note: Already deployed as a blind objective; also a fine printed meld.

name: FEMA Mode
effect: Once enough weather hazards have struck, disaster relief arrives - the fame goal drops for the rest of the run.
note: Compensation that accumulates, so a run of bad levels becomes a good story.

name: Row Card
effect: Gives points to its whole row when it scores.
note: Shipped in spirit as the row bucket.

name: Score the Entrance
effect: Cards still in the Entrance when the show ends are scored too.
note: Turns held cards into value instead of waste. A good rule card.

name: Earthquake
effect: The board is scrambled - every placed card moves to a different cell in its own grid.
note: Total spatial reset as a hazard rather than as a card.

name: Tornado
effect: A tornado of a random scale lifts a square area of cards and drops them elsewhere.
note: Scaled damage, so the same blind can be small or enormous.

name: Eruption
effect: Burning spreads outward in an expanding snake with no way to stop it.
note: The unanswerable hazard - the counterplay is to score fast, not to prevent it.

name: Monopoly Rule
effect: Scoring a flush of a rank removes that rank from future generation for the rest of the run.
note: Self-limiting play - your best line becomes unavailable by using it.

name: Wildfire
effect: Fire spreads through flammable cards and is stopped by cards of a named blocking type.
note: Terrain matters - the player builds firebreaks out of their own cards.

name: Windy Day
effect: Cards shift one row or column at random because it is too windy to hold them.
note: Small, constant, and it makes exact formations expensive.

name: Mini Metro Mode
effect: Completed straights become metro lines whose ends are stations, and the lines must carry passengers over several refills.
note: A whole alternate mode built on the meld the game already detects.

name: Boss Fight
effect: A boss appears that must be beaten with specific hands or with raw points, and it breathes fire on your score while you work.
note: A score that goes down as well as up, which changes the whole pacing of a show.

name: Vampires
effect: Vampires begin eating cards from the edge of the board inward and must all be played over to be removed.
note: Attacks the edges, which is where the diagonals and the long rows live.

name: The Impostor
effect: One card in the deck is fake - it loses you score when played, and on some refills it ignores the rules entirely. Find it and remove it.
note: Deduction as counterplay. The best hazard in the list.

name: Timeline Clash
effect: Send a card into the past and replay that board forward to the present, where the timelines clash and only the differences survive.
note: Absurd, memorable, and the undo system already stores the history it would need.

name: Earth type
effect: Stays at the bottom of the deck.
note: One of the four elemental deck-position types.

name: Air type
effect: Stays at the top of the deck.
note: One of the four elemental deck-position types.

name: Water type
effect: Moves one position down the deck each refill.
note: Remapped from the drop-down version, which is superseded in the catalog.

name: Fire type
effect: Moves one position up the deck each refill.
note: The fourth elemental deck-position type.

name: Money suit
effect: Gold cards act as money at shops and are worth their full trade value.
note: Shipped as the Gold type after the owner's ruling that it works better as a type than a suit.

name: Discard-deck verbs
effect: Ways to reach into the discard - recur a card, reorder it, or score from it.
note: The one taxonomy family the draft names only in the effects grid, not in the draft prose.

name: Card-gain verbs
effect: Ways to gain cards mid-show, as opposed to buying them.
note: Distinct from the shop; these are the effects that make a deck grow during play.

name: Seals family
effect: The seal family, renamed stamps and then hats - modifiers attached to a card rather than replacing its skill.
note: Three shipped: Double Trigger, Revealing, Global.

name: Disaster brainstorm provenance
effect: The disaster column of the random-effects sheet is a pasted chat brainstorm, timestamps and all - weather, bosses and mode ideas that became most of the hazard blinds.
note: The timestamps and handles are transcript artefacts, not ideas. Recorded so the empty-looking cells are explained rather than lost.

name: Recommendations companion
effect: A companion to the design record holding interpretation and invention, kept separate so it never contaminates what the owner actually designed. Its implementation remarks predate the shipped spotlight, map, props and combo formula.
note: The separation is the reason this file exists too - mined ideas stay labelled as mined.

name: Spatial deckbuilding pillar
effect: Position is the game's differentiator - every card should ask a placement question, not just a selection question.
note: The grid overhaul is this pillar taken seriously. Spiderweb, rings, props and formations are its best expressions.

name: Rule deck as content engine
effect: The rule deck is not architectural elegance, it is where boss debuffs, ascensions, secret melds and unlocks all live.
note: Confirmed by the blinds category, which needed no new system at all.

name: Tour fantasy pillar
effect: A route is a story, which solves the campaign-for-Tetris problem - the map is the narrative layer.
note: The third pillar, and the reason the map is worth its cost.

name: Deferred systems
effect: Deferred - quests, event-recycled prestige, lore scraps, cosmetics, the empty-rule-deck deck, mana cards.
note: All fine, none needed for the core loop, per the owner's own retention essay.

name: Cut the rarity chain
effect: Cut - cards that only raise the odds of other rarities. They are dead cards touching only the meta layer, and they fight the cards-as-currency economy.
note: Fold luck manipulation into the Fortune Teller class, where it has a face.

name: Summary-card rulings
effect: Adopt Ghost Card as a stamp, The Acrobat, and Searing Knife; reject The Anarchist and Sliced Reality.
note: The Anarchist becomes a blind rather than a player card; column-count changes are already ZoneAdder's job.

name: The combo reframe
effect: Effects supply the points and melds supply the multiplier, keeping both axes - show score is the sum of effect points times one plus the row combo times one plus the column combo.
note: Adopted in shape. The shipped three-bucket product is this formula with the special bucket added.

name: The audience is the antagonist
effect: Do not add an enemy with a health bar - the goal score already is one. Fame needed, tips for overscoring, cheers per combo.
note: The Slay the Spire feel for zero new systems.

name: Rings as depth multipliers
effect: Performance rings multiply the column combo by depth, rewarding the riskiest behaviour - covering your own cards.
note: The tension between deep columns and the spotlight is named here as the game itself. Protect it.

name: Formalise The Booking
effect: A tour is won by fulfilling contracts, not by maximum score - score X with no knife melds, finish in two acts, trigger twelve unique feats.
note: Unifies mini-game events, boss blinds and the optimisation essay into one diegetic object.

name: Fix the spotlight first
effect: Every skill is dead until active-while-unblocked works, and covered becomes a resource once it does.
note: Shipped since. The advice to re-evaluate the whole catalog afterwards is what this rewrite is doing.

name: Four suits plus specials
effect: Four base suits - Knives, Hoops, Balls, Flames - with Clowns and Dancers as classes and Fireworks and Electric as special suits found only through packs.
note: CONTRADICTED by the newer draft line calling for five base suits. The draft is newer, so five wins unless the owner says otherwise.

name: The Joey rank
effect: Jacks become Joeys and count as Clown-class cards.
note: Vetoed in the catalog - a rank that is always eleven is boring, and the Joey should be a clown token with a real effect.

name: The Ringmistress rank
effect: Queens become Ringmistresses and count as Producer-class cards.
note: Vetoed in the catalog; the historical reference can be recycled onto a real card.

name: The Impresario rank
effect: Kings become Impresarios, count as Producer cards and add trade value at shops.
note: Vetoed in the catalog; the reference can be recycled.

name: The Headliner rank
effect: Aces count high or low in runs, decided in your favour at evaluation.
note: Vetoed as a rank rename, but the high-or-low duality is a real spatial decision worth keeping on some card.

name: Harlequin pip
effect: Counts as two suits at once for every comparison, meld and suit effect, firing both props.
note: Vetoed by the owner as boring. The multi-suit stub in the comparator remains, so the mechanism survives the veto.

name: The Gaff
effect: Shows a fixed rank and suit until it scores, then reveals its true random value.
note: Sideshow slang for a faked exhibit. The reveal is the payoff, and the Prepared Town blind is its counter.

name: Half-step rank
effect: Rank five and a half - stacks between five and six but never melds.
note: Owner note - it makes more sense as a hat than as a rank. Same effect, different slot.

name: The Fifteen rank
effect: Also melds with any neighbours whose ranks sum to fifteen with it.
note: Made into a talent rather than a rank, per the owner. It is the demoted cribbage rule given a home.

name: Roman numeral rank
effect: Cosmetic rank skin that melds normally.
note: Accepted. Circus Maximus is where the word circus comes from, so the skin is on-theme.

name: The Blank rank
effect: No rank, no suit - stacks on anything, anything stacks on it, and it scores nothing.
note: Accepted. Free spatial glue that teaches position is not points.

name: Canvas type
effect: The sturdy default for circus-born cards, an upgrade of Paper.
note: Establishes a material progression rather than a single default.

name: Sawdust type
effect: When discarded, leaves a marker on its cell; the next card placed there scores extra.
note: Makes discarding spatial, which the discard-engine essay needs.

name: Rosin type
effect: Sticky - cards placed on it can never be picked up again, but score deeper into the ring bands.
note: The cards-that-resist-being-moved note, given a reason to exist: commitment for reward.

name: Tintype type
effect: On acquisition, permanently copies the pips of the card it was made from.
note: Duplication with lineage. Collectors will chase photographs of photographs.

name: Lithograph type
effect: While in the Entrance rather than in a grid, this card broadcasts its skill globally.
note: A card that wants not to be played, which inverts the whole game's incentive. The Entrance is row -1, so this still works exactly as written.

name: Glass type
effect: Double points when scored; shatters after three scores.
note: Balatro-proven risk and reward, and the timer creates a last-show-for-this-card moment.

name: Wax type
effect: Melts near Flames - loses rank each show it shares a column with a Flames card.
note: Anti-synergy as flavour, and the waxworks really did burn down twice.

name: Ticket Stub type
effect: Spent as currency at shops for a discount; worthless in the Ring.
note: Gives cards-as-currency a small denomination.

name: Flash type
effect: Scores triple, but only the first time it would score in a show.
note: Juggling slang for throwing every prop once. Rewards choreographing when a card enters scoring.

name: Spangle stamp
effect: Adds to the combo when this card is part of any meld.
note: The common-tier workhorse every build wants.

name: Greasepaint stamp
effect: This card counts as a Clown in addition to its own class.
note: The class-splashing enabler every tribal system needs.

name: Top Billing stamp
effect: This card always scores first within its meld.
note: Trigger order is invisible depth; this stamp makes it player-facing.

name: Understudy stamp
effect: If the card above it in the stack is destroyed or consumed, this card copies its skill.
note: Turns destruction effects into setup plays. The flip made above the correct direction.

name: Lloyd's Policy stamp
effect: The first time this card would be destroyed or debuffed, prevent it.
note: Insurance against the game's own debuff system, and performers really did insure body parts.

name: Ghost Light stamp
effect: Does not block the spotlight of cards beneath it.
note: The counterweight the ring-depth tension needs - build tall without killing your engines.

name: The Encore stamp
effect: If this card's skill triggered this show, it has a chance to trigger once more at show end.
note: The end-of-show lottery tick.

name: Contract Ink stamp
effect: Pays extra per show it is played, and leaves the deck if benched two shows running.
note: Anti-autopilot pressure, and performers really did jump between rival shows.

name: The Egress
effect: Cue to send any card on the board straight to the discard and gain a Ticket Stub.
note: Targeted removal plus an economy trickle, and the joke lands every time.

name: Humbug
effect: Counts as a copy of the most valuable card in its row while covered, and reveals as rank two when spotlit.
note: Inverts the spotlight - a card you want covered. The best placement puzzle in the set.

name: White Elephant
effect: Huge points when scored, but eats a Gold card every show it stays in the deck.
note: A cost-over-time bomb; when to finally dump it is a real decision.

name: The Red Wagon
effect: While spotlit, every Gold card in the deck counts as a wildcard toward every column run.
note: The economy-to-scoring pivot - the yak-shave moment in card form.

name: Pink Lemonade
effect: When a Flames card and a Concessions card score in the same row, gain a bonus and draw.
note: Teaches cross-class rows, and the origin legend is worth the flavour text.

name: Sawing in Half
effect: Cue to split a card into two cards of half rank, rounded apart, same suit.
note: Rank arithmetic as a tool - fabricate runs on demand.

name: Clown Car
effect: At each refill, draw an extra card into this card's column, and one more per Clown that scored last refill.
note: An escalating tempo engine where the board literally overflows with clowns.

name: Custard Pie
effect: Cue to change a target card's suit to Balls; if that completes a flush row, gain a multiplier.
note: Suit fixing with a payoff condition, which makes it feel like aiming.

name: The Leotard
effect: Cue to move this card and everything above it to any cell, legal or not.
note: Stack teleport, which breaks placement rules the way the trapeze breaks gravity.

name: Blondin's Crossing
effect: Once per show, move an entire row one cell left or right, wrapping.
note: The biggest single spatial verb in the game, and wrapping now means crossing into the next grid.

name: Jumbo
effect: Heavy - nothing may be placed on Jumbo, Jumbo may be placed on anything, and it scores per card beneath it.
note: A stack-capper with weight you can feel. It ends a stack deliberately.

name: Flea Circus
effect: Counts as five cards of rank one for combo purposes.
note: Tiny card, huge combo. The joke is the mechanic.

name: Liberty Horses
effect: At each refill, every Animal card in the Entrance rearranges itself into ascending order.
note: Auto-sorting is deeply satisfying, and the Entrance is exactly where order matters now.

name: Mabel's Tigers
effect: Consumes the card it is dropped on, but only prop cards, gaining rank with each meal.
note: A curved Gluttony - eats your chaff, thins the deck, respects feats.

name: Straitjacket
effect: Starts each show unable to be moved and frees itself, scoring, when its line scores.
note: A self-solving problem where the escape is the payoff.

name: Milk Can
effect: Cue to put a card inside - it is out of play until you retrieve it on any later refill.
note: A pocket dimension, which is a tempo tool for holding a combo piece.

name: Wall of Death
effect: Adjacent columns gain a multiplier, and cards in them take an Exhaust debuff each show.
note: An aura with a cost, where placement decides who pays it.

name: The Seance Buster
effect: Reveals every Gaff, Humbug and disguised card on the board and scores per fake revealed.
note: Counterplay that makes fakes a real subgame. Houdini against the mediums is history's best rivalry.

name: The Tarot Reading
effect: Cue to look at the top five cards of the deck and reorder them.
note: The scry every deck game needs, and here the order decides which cell each card can reach.

name: Madame Zora's Eye
effect: The next card to be drawn is always visible above the deck.
note: Permanent information that changes every refill decision. Quiet and beloved.

name: The Major Arcana
effect: Twenty-two unique one-shot consumables, each a spatial verb - destroy a column, reroll a row's ranks, flip a stack.
note: A collectible sub-set, which is long-term chase content built from verbs the grid already has.

name: Grand Spec
effect: If every column of a grid scored this show, double that show's combo.
note: The perfect-show fantasy button, and the spec really was the whole company parading.

name: Drumroll
effect: The last meld scored this refill gains a multiplier.
note: Trigger order matters again, and it pairs directly with Top Billing.

name: Fairy Floss
effect: When scored, adjacent cards gain a rank for the rest of the show.
note: Adjacency buff as a placement puzzle. Cotton candy was co-invented by a dentist.

name: The Grease Joint
effect: At show start, feed the bottom card of the deck to the discard and draw one.
note: Deck-bottom filtering, which no other effect touches.

name: Peanut Pitch
effect: Cue with three charges to add points to any one card, thrown from anywhere.
note: The charge system's tutorial card.

name: The Equestrian
effect: Leader whose melds scored in the first ring band gain a multiplier.
note: Philip Astley, who standardised the forty-two foot ring in 1768 and invented the modern circus.

name: The Showman
effect: Leader whose shops offer an extra card and whose Gaff and Humbug cards cost nothing.
note: Barnum. The deception build's patron.

name: The Escapologist
effect: Leader who doubles your free undo and shortens every debuff by one show.
note: Houdini. The blind-resistant leader.

name: The Aerialist
effect: Leader who rescores the topmost meld once per refill, and is destroyed if her column ever fails to score.
note: Lillian Leitzel, Ringling's biggest star, killed by a rigging failure. The fragility is the history.

name: The Tiger Queen
effect: Leader for whom consumption effects have no cap.
note: Mabel Stark, who worked big cats into her seventies.

name: The Sibyl
effect: Leader whose deck top is always revealed and whose first shop reroll is free.
note: The midway mitt-camp fortune teller.

name: The Cannon King
effect: Leader whose Fireworks cards may score from inside the Entrance.
note: The Zacchini human-cannonball dynasty. Scoring from row -1 is a genuinely new privilege.

name: The Sweet Tooth
effect: Leader for whom every rank buff is permanent rather than per-show.
note: The cotton-candy dentist.

name: The Costumier
effect: Leader whose cards may hold two stamps.
note: The wardrobe mistresses of the great shows.

name: The Sharpshooter
effect: Leader who names a rank each show; that rank scores double.
note: Annie Oakley shot holes through playing cards, and free tickets are still called Annie Oakleys.

name: The Route Book
effect: The run's planning and summary screen, named for the route books circuses published each season; deviating from the planned path costs fame.
note: Gives the tour-planning idea a real object and a real cost.

name: The Advance Man
effect: A map consumable that reveals fogged nodes ahead.
note: Billposters really did travel weeks ahead of the show. The counter to limited route vision.

name: Paper the House
effect: Auto-pass a town's fame check and earn no tips - free tickets to look popular.
note: A skip button with a cost, which is exactly what a long tour needs.

name: Straw House
effect: When tips exceed a threshold, the next node's offers gain a rarity tier.
note: A sold-out show where straw was laid for extra seating. The overscore reward, named.

name: Winter Quarters
effect: The between-run hub, named for the Baraboo and Sarasota tradition where circuses rebuilt, trained and planned.
note: Better than Carnival - prestige spending becomes literally preparing next season.

name: The White Elephant War
effect: A rival gifts you a White Elephant - take it, or insult them and face a harder Rival Show.
note: Barnum against Forepaugh, 1884. A gift that is also a trap.

name: The Egress event
effect: A mysterious sign. Follow it and skip this node entirely - no reward, no risk.
note: Barnum's museum sign, and a genuinely useful escape hatch.

name: First of May
effect: A rookie joins - gain a random Common with a hidden growth condition that upgrades it once it has scored ten times.
note: Circus slang for a first-season performer. The hidden condition is the hook.

name: Cutting Up Jackpots
effect: Old troupers swap tall tales - reroll any one card in your deck into another of the same class.
note: Slang for swapping exaggerated war stories.

name: Cherry Pie
effect: Extra work for extra pay - take a debuff card for this show and gain Gold cards.
note: Slang for extra paid crew work. A blind you choose.

name: The Museum of Humbugs
effect: Buy a Gaff cheap - it might be real, with a small chance of being a Legendary.
note: The Fiji Mermaid and the Cardiff Giant, and a sucker born every minute.

name: Seance Night
effect: Pick the Gaff out of three face-down cards for a reward.
note: Houdini against the spiritualists, as a small deduction game.

name: The Pie Car
effect: A rest node - heal one debuff, or gamble at the crew's rigged three-card monte.
note: The circus train's diner and social car.

name: The Erdnase Cipher
effect: An author signature that appears on random cards across many runs; collecting and scoring all of them unlocks something never explained.
note: Erdnase wrote card handling's bible in 1902 and his identity is still unknown. Never explain it.

name: The Forty-Two Foot Ring
effect: A secret meld that fires when a grid's row and column scores total exactly forty-two.
note: Astley's ring is forty-two feet because of horse physics. Hide the number everywhere.

name: The Three Rings
effect: Score three separate five-card rows in one show to permanently unlock an extra grid rule card.
note: A secret meld whose reward is more board, which is the best reward this game has.

name: The Sword Swallower meld
effect: A column that is one perfect descending run from top to bottom.
note: A secret meld the player can stumble into and then chase deliberately.

name: The Ghost Show
effect: After midnight by the real clock, the menu wagon's lights are out and one secret card can be found only then.
note: Spook shows - midnight horror performances in circus tents - are real history.

name: Variable-ratio rewards
effect: Pack mulligans, The Encore, Bullet Catch, Gaff reveals and the Museum of Humbugs are all variable-ratio schedules; lean into near-miss presentation.
note: Show what you almost pulled. The strongest reinforcement schedule known.

name: Near-miss and loss aversion
effect: Bookings make failure specific - missed by forty - rather than vague, manufacturing Balatro's one-hand-left panic every show.
note: The argument for The Booking being a headline feature rather than a card.

name: Spatial mastery
effect: A skilled player wins boards a weak player loses with the identical deck, which is replay depth no amount of content buys.
note: The reason effects should keep referencing position rather than raw arithmetic.

name: The pivot loop
effect: Every run should offer one card that makes the player abandon their plan - leaders for identity, Greasepaint for splashing, The Red Wagon for the economy pivot, Calliope for rainbow.
note: The yak-shave note, turned into a content requirement.

name: Collection and completion
effect: The Major Arcana series, unlocked leaders, route-book stamps and the achievement pass retain players between runs.
note: Completion pressure is the between-session hook.

name: Narrative for free
effect: Every card ships with a true story, so flavour text supplies the lore without writing a campaign.
note: The circus already wrote it. This is why every row in this file names a referent.

name: Session shape
effect: Short shows, medium tours, long route book and hub - three interlocking loops make the one-more ladder.
note: The show length changed with the overhaul; the three-loop shape did not.

name: Build order
effect: Spotlight, then the scoring formula, then the map, then a forty-card First Season set, then the economy, then the meta layer - each step makes the previous one testable in context.
note: The first three have shipped. The First Season set is what this CSV rewrite is feeding.

name: The Joey leader
effect: Leader granting one free Slapstick - a swap of two adjacent ranks - every refill.
note: Joseph Grimaldi, Regency London's superstar clown and the reason clowns are still called Joeys.

name: Recommendations document map
effect: The companion's section map - how the design reads, the resolved questions, then new suits and pips, types, stamps, skills by class, leaders, towns, events, secrets, the retention argument and the build order.
note: Section headings and table headers, kept so the file's shape is legible without opening it.

name: Class table headers
effect: Each skill class gets its own table - Producer, Magician, Clown, Acrobat, Animal Trainer, Escape Artist, Fortune Teller, Special Effects and Concessions - with rarity, effect, source and why it is fun.
note: The nine class tables' headings and column rows. The class list itself is the taxonomy the catalog's groups column uses.

name: Roster table headers
effect: The leader roster, the towns and hazards table, the events table and the secrets list each carry their own heading and column row.
note: Structural lines from the second half of the companion.

name: The compendium is a quarry
effect: A worldwide reference file of circus, magic, sideshow, fairground, street performance, gambling and card culture, each entry mapped to the kind of effect it could become. Nothing in it is committed design.
note: Its hook vocabulary matches the game's systems, which is what makes it minable rather than merely interesting.

name: Learned Pigs and Fireflies
effect: Ricky Jay's compendium of history's strangest performers, named as the spiritual ancestor of the whole reference file.
note: If one reference sends you further, let it be that one.

name: Beni Hasan jugglers
effect: The oldest depiction of juggling, from an Egyptian tomb around 1994 BCE - the origin card for the Balls suit.
note: The suit already ships; this is its provenance.

name: Dedi
effect: The magician of the Westcar Papyrus, who reattached severed heads - a card that restores a destroyed card to the board intact.
note: Restoration is rarer than destruction and should stay that way.

name: Acetabularii
effect: Rome's cups-and-balls performers - shuffle the positions of face-down cards.
note: The oldest continuously performed trick on Earth.

name: Bull-leaping
effect: Minoan acrobats vaulting a charging bull - move over a hazard card and score for surviving it.
note: Around 1500 BCE, and the earliest recorded danger act.

name: Circus Maximus
effect: A chariot-racing arena for a quarter of a million spectators - the name the whole genre borrowed.
note: The fame-goal ceiling as a boss town.

name: Venationes
effect: Staged beast hunts and flooded arenas - a level whose board is prefilled with hazard cards.
note: Roman state games, which is where spectacle-as-politics starts.

name: Bread and Circuses
effect: Give a free show to keep the town content - no fame, but the next node's prices drop.
note: Juvenal's sneer, four words that still describe the business.

name: Hippodrome Factions
effect: Blues and Greens - two factions in the crowd, each demanding a different half of the board score.
note: Chariot fandoms so powerful they became political parties and started a riot that burned the city.

name: Funambulus
effect: The Latin for rope-walker, still the technical term - the wire-crossing card's proper name.
note: Petauristarii were the acrobats; funambulus the rope-walker.

name: Baixi
effect: The Hundred Entertainments of Han China around 200 BCE - the umbrella spectacle of acrobatics, pole climbing and illusion.
note: The oldest evidence that variety, not a single act, is the format.

name: Sword Swallowing origin
effect: Ascetic demonstrations of bodily control from India, by tradition around 2000 BCE - swallow the card above you.
note: The provenance for the Sword Swallower card.

name: Jongleurs
effect: Itinerant do-everything performers - a card that counts as three different classes at once but scores less in each.
note: The medieval generalist, and the argument that variety predates specialisation.

name: The Fool's License
effect: The one performer permitted to mock the king - while in play, one restriction from the blind is ignored.
note: Truth wrapped in folly, and the cleanest counterplay card in the file.

name: The Marotte
effect: The jester's sceptre topped with a miniature of his own head - this card carries a miniature copy of its own skill that triggers separately.
note: A stamp that duplicates rather than modifies.

name: Lord of Misrule
effect: Sanctioned role reversal - for one show, commons score as legendaries and legendaries as commons.
note: The Feast of Fools, where a peasant was crowned and hierarchy inverted for a day.

name: Charivari
effect: The clowns' opening tumbling rush, from the mock-parade of pot-banging - the show's opening animation across the board.
note: The word survived from folk ritual into circus vocabulary intact.

name: Commedia stock characters
effect: Arlecchino, Colombina, Pantalone and the rest - touring troupes of masked stock characters, the direct ancestor of clown archetypes.
note: A whole cast whose relationships are already written.

name: Mr Punch
effect: The hook-nosed Neapolitan puppet who became England's Punch - destroys an adjacent card and scores, every time, without consequence.
note: That is the way to do it. A card that gets away with it is genuinely funny.

name: Till Eulenspiegel
effect: The prankster who takes every instruction maliciously literally - this card fulfils the letter of a blind's objective in the least useful way and still scores.
note: A card built on rules-lawyering, which the rule deck makes possible.

name: Pageant Wagons
effect: Bible plays staged on wagons rolling street to street - a mobile stage that carries its board between nodes.
note: The tour structure, five centuries early.

name: Bartholomew Fair
effect: Seven centuries of England's wildest fair - rope-dancers, monsters, puppets and every attraction at once.
note: The template for a city node containing several attractions.

name: Mountebanks
effect: Renaissance stage-medicine sellers - cue to sell a card whose effect is not what was advertised.
note: The ancestors of the medicine show, and of the Potion Seller card.

name: Skomorokhi
effect: Russian minstrel-clowns with bears and gusli, banned and persecuted by church and tsar - a town where one class is outlawed outright.
note: The ban-workaround family's oldest entry.

name: Jacob Hall
effect: The celebrity rope-dancer of Restoration London, name-dropped by Pepys - an early famous body.
note: Naming source for a wire card.

name: The Conjurer
effect: Bosch's painting of a cups-and-balls show where an accomplice picks the absorbed spectator's pocket - this card steals while an adjacent card holds attention.
note: A two-card combo painted in 1502.

name: The Discoverie of Witchcraft
effect: Reginald Scot exposed conjuring methods in 1584 to save accused witches from execution - reveal every hidden card on the board.
note: Exposure as mercy. Better history than any invented flavour.

name: Golden-age additions
effect: Astley, Barnum, Bailey, Grimaldi, Leitzel, Kelly, Jacobs, the Wallendas and Oakley are placed in the recommendations; this section adds what those missed.
note: The two files divide the golden age between them deliberately.

name: John Bill Ricketts
effect: The first American circus, 1793 - George Washington attended and sold him a horse.
note: An event where a famous patron gifts you a card.

name: The Courier of St Petersburg
effect: Ducrow's signature act, standing astride multiple horses at once - this card occupies two adjacent cells and scores in both lines.
note: A card that straddles two columns, which is a genuinely new geometry.

name: Pablo Fanque
effect: The first Black British circus proprietor, whose 1843 poster the Beatles lifted verbatim for Mr Kite.
note: A leader whose poster is his signature - the billing itself is the effect.

name: Lord George Sanger
effect: The showman who awarded himself a peerage in answer to Buffalo Bill's Honourable - this card promotes itself a rarity tier and charges accordingly.
note: Self-conferred status as a mechanic.

name: Carl Hagenbeck
effect: Revolutionised animal acts with reward-based gentling instead of fear, and invented the cageless enclosure - a leader whose Animal cards never need a trainer adjacent.
note: The humane alternative, and historically the more successful one.

name: Jenny Lind hype
effect: Barnum pre-sold a singer America had never heard into a national mania - declare a card as the headline before the show and it scores double if it scores at all.
note: Advance hype as a wager, which is The Booking pointed at a card.

name: Tom Thumb's Wedding
effect: The media event of 1863 - even Lincoln sent word.
note: A wedding event pairing two cards permanently, so they always draw together.

name: Bailey's Electric Light
effect: Bailey lit the circus with electricity before most towns had it - the show arrived carrying its own daylight.
note: The night-show rule, sourced.

name: The Seven-Person Pyramid
effect: The Wallendas' seven-person pyramid, and its 1962 collapse - a stack of seven that scores enormously and falls entirely if any card is removed.
note: The most famous formation in circus history, with its failure mode included.

name: Con Colleano
effect: The Wizard of the Wire, first to land a feet-to-feet forward somersault on the tightwire.
note: The forward somersault card's historical anchor.

name: Bird Millman
effect: The Ziegfeld-era wire dancer - a Dancer-class card that moves along a row while scoring formations.
note: Naming source for the wire-dancer card.

name: Gargantua
effect: Ringling's acid-scarred gorilla, whose forced grin was billed as ferocity - a card whose printed threat is entirely marketing and whose real effect is gentle.
note: Marketing genius and animal cruelty in the same act. Handle the framing carefully.

name: Chang and Eng Bunker
effect: The original conjoined twins, who toured on their own terms and became successful businessmen - two cards that must be placed adjacent and score as one.
note: They controlled their own billing, which is the part worth telling.

name: Anna Swan and Martin Bates
effect: The giantess and the giant who married - two cards that score for their combined height in a stack.
note: Nearly fifteen feet together.

name: Johnny Eck
effect: The Amazing Half-Boy - performer, artist and illusion-builder with his twin. A card that occupies only the upper half of a cell, leaving room beneath.
note: Half a cell is a new placement geometry.

name: Prince Randian
effect: The Human Torso, who rolled and lit cigarettes with his lips across forty-five years - a card that produces a token every refill using nothing.
note: The Human Cigarette Factory's real name.

name: Violet and Daisy Hilton
effect: Conjoined-twin vaudeville stars with saxophone and jazz - this card doubles an adjacent card's trigger when both score together.
note: Twin harmony as a mechanic.

name: Annie Jones
effect: Barnum's bearded lady, who led the performers' campaign to abolish the word freak.
note: An event where the troupe renames itself, changing a class name for the rest of the run.

name: Betty Broadbent
effect: The tattooed lady - five hundred and sixty-five tattoos across forty years. The Illustrated card holds several stamps at once.
note: The multi-stamp card, with a real body behind it.

name: The Living Skeleton and the Fat Lady
effect: Battersby and Perkins, the sideshow's beloved odd couple - two cards whose ranks average when they are adjacent.
note: Averaging is a verb nothing else in the game has.

name: Zip the Pinhead
effect: Sixty years performing a mystery Barnum never explained - a card whose effect is never written on it and never told.
note: The purest secret card the game could print.

name: One of Us
effect: The initiation chant from the 1932 film - the troupe accepts an outsider.
note: An event where a card gains a class it did not have.

name: The Talker and the Bally
effect: The talker - never barker - worked the bally platform outside; the blow-off was the extra-charge finale inside.
note: Precise vocabulary for the shop and the pack-opening screens.

name: Ten-in-One
effect: Ten acts under one tent, a single-attraction show, or a continuous grind show - the three sideshow formats.
note: Three node shapes with historical names already attached.

name: The Durov Dynasty
effect: Animal-trainer clowns famed for kindness-based training and political satire.
note: A leader who is both Clown and Animal Trainer, which no other card is.

name: Moscow State Circus
effect: The USSR industrialised circus with state academies and guaranteed employment - the opposite of the touring gamble.
note: A meta-progression model where training replaces buying.

name: Oleg Popov
effect: The Sunshine Clown, gentle and wordless, beloved across the Cold War divide - a card that removes one negative status from every card in its grid.
note: Kindness as a mechanic, which the game has too little of.

name: Yuri Nikulin
effect: The clown so beloved he became a film star and ran the Moscow circus.
note: A Clown leader whose signature is fame rather than mischief.

name: Karandash
effect: The Pencil, the USSR's defining clown, with his dog Klyaksa - the Inkblot. A card that draws a permanent mark on a cell.
note: A clown who leaves marks on the board is a good fit for the cell-modifier family.

name: Bear Cycling
effect: The iconic and now ethically fraught Soviet image of bears on bicycles.
note: Visual reference only, with the ethical note kept attached.

name: Dzhigitovka
effect: Cossack trick riding - hanging off the saddle at full gallop to pick objects off the ground. This card collects a card from a cell it passes without stopping.
note: Movement plus collection in one verb.

name: Wuqiao County
effect: The hometown of acrobatics, where the trade has been every family's for centuries.
note: A starting deck whose cards all share one class, sourced to a real place.

name: Plate Spinning
effect: Dozens of plates kept alive by returning to each in turn - a mechanic where cards decay unless revisited.
note: Attention as a resource, which the patience system also reaches for.

name: Hoop Diving and Chair Stacking
effect: Precision diving through towers of hoops, and chairs balanced to the ceiling - a card that scores for the height of the stack it dives through.
note: The Chinese source for both the hoop suit and the height coordinate.

name: Diabolo
effect: The Chinese yo-yo - a card juggled between two columns, scoring in both while it travels.
note: Centuries old and now global.

name: Lion Dance
effect: Two performers inside one lion, pole-jumping in the southern style - two cards that move as one unit.
note: Paired movement, which is distinct from paired scoring.

name: The Dragon Meld
effect: A whole team animating one long dragon - a run that, once assembled, moves along the board as a single body.
note: The longest meld in the game, and the only one that then moves.

name: Bian Lian
effect: Sichuan face-changing - masks swapped in an instant, the technique so guarded it is passed only within families. A card that changes its suit and rank between one glance and the next.
note: The secrecy is part of the act, so the card should never explain how.

name: Sun Wukong
effect: The Monkey King's seventy-two transformations - a card that becomes any other card on the board, once per refill.
note: The acrobat role of Chinese opera, and the best copy card available.

name: You Meng
effect: The jester of Chu, who impersonated a dead minister so movingly the king restored his family's fortune - a card that copies a card removed from play.
note: Impersonation as advocacy, around 600 BCE.

name: Hard Qigong
effect: Iron-head and spear-against-throat demonstrations - a card that cannot be destroyed while it is spotlit.
note: Conditioning as armour.

name: Piyingxi
effect: Chinese leather shadow puppets against lamplit screens, a thousand years old.
note: A visual treatment for the card-art pop-up.

name: The Leaf Game
effect: The Tang dynasty yezi ge, the earliest known playing cards, ninth century.
note: The First Deck as a secret - the oldest card in the game, findable once.

name: Money-Suited Cards
effect: Early Chinese decks used currency as suits - coins, strings of coins, myriads.
note: The historical precedent for the Gold suit, and the reason it works.

name: Misemono
effect: Edo spectacle booths of curiosities, crafts and feats - Japan's own sideshow culture.
note: A node name with its own aesthetic.

name: Daikagura
effect: Lion dance and juggling as a Shinto blessing - juggling as literal purification. This card clears every negative status from the line it scores in.
note: Sacred juggling, which recasts the Balls suit entirely.

name: Kyokugoma
effect: Edo virtuoso top-spinning; Matsui Gensui toured the West in the 1860s. A spinning card that keeps its effect alive for several refills.
note: A timed effect with a visible spin-down.

name: The Butterfly Trick
effect: Japan's most famous classical conjuring piece - paper butterflies kept aloft by a fan. A prop that stays airborne over the board until it lands.
note: Sustained rather than instantaneous props.

name: Shokyokusai Tenkatsu
effect: The superstar female magician of Meiji and Taisho Japan, who ran her own troupe.
note: The Magician leader.

name: Karakuri Ningyo
effect: Edo clockwork automata - the tea-serving doll that trundles to a guest and waits. A card type that moves itself to a target and stops.
note: Self-moving cards with a destination, not a direction.

name: Bunraku
effect: Three visible operators animating one puppet, with total audience buy-in - three cards that jointly control a fourth.
note: A four-card formation that nothing else in the game resembles.

name: Kuroko
effect: The black-clad stagehands the audience agrees not to see - this card does not block the spotlight beneath it and cannot itself be targeted.
note: Already sketched in the pre-grid curated file. The agreement not to see is the mechanic.

name: Hikinuki
effect: Kabuki quick-change - a costume ripped away mid-dance to reveal a new character. This card changes into a different card when its line scores.
note: Transformation timed to the moment of maximum attention.

name: Mie
effect: The frozen cross-eyed climax pose, held while the audience shouts the actor's name.
note: The pose a card should strike when its effect fires - the effect-art pop-up, given a form.

name: Chindon'ya
effect: Costumed street bands hired to advertise shops - cue to raise the next node's rewards.
note: Walking hype, purchasable.

name: Hanafuda
effect: Flower cards born from repeated gambling bans - each ban spawned a new disguised design, and Nintendo began by printing them.
note: The ban-workaround family's best story, and a deck whose identity is evasion.

name: Ya-Ku-Za
effect: Eight-nine-three, the worst hand in oicho-kabu, and the source of the word yakuza.
note: A secret meld that pays for scoring the worst possible hand.

name: Competitive Karuta
effect: Lightning-reflex card snatching to recited poetry.
note: A timed duel event, and the one minigame with a real-world rulebook.

name: Sarumawashi
effect: Street monkey-trainer performances, a thousand years old - a token that climbs the stack and returns.
note: A token with a route rather than a target.

name: Mallakhamb
effect: The wrestler's pole - gymnastics performed wrapped around a wooden pole, which makes the column itself the apparatus.
note: The clearest historical argument that a column is a piece of equipment.

name: The Great Indian Rope Trick
effect: The most famous trick that probably never existed, largely a newspaper invention of 1890 - a card whose effect is only described, never seen.
note: A legendary whose whole point is that nobody can prove it happened.

name: The Basket Trick
effect: A performer vanishes into a basket run through with swords and reappears unharmed in the crowd - a card removed from play that returns to a different cell.
note: Removal and return, with the swords as the reason it reads as risk.

name: The Mango Seed
effect: A seed grows into a fruiting tree in minutes under a cloth - a rank-one card that grows while covered.
note: An anti-spotlight card that wants to be buried.

name: Jadoo-Wallahs
effect: Hereditary street conjurers performing without stage or lighting.
note: Naming and art source for the Magician class's street tier.

name: P C Sorcar
effect: India's great showman-magician, whose 1956 BBC sawing ran past the broadcast cutoff and left a nation believing it had watched a death.
note: A card whose effect resolves one refill later than expected, on purpose.

name: Snake Charming
effect: The been and the swaying cobra, which responds to motion rather than to music - a card that pulls another along its column by moving.
note: The correction is the good detail: it follows the instrument, not the tune.

name: Bahurupiya
effect: Of many forms - quick-change impersonators who arrive each day as a different god, animal or official.
note: A card that is a different class every refill.

name: Nat and Dombari
effect: Hereditary acrobat communities and village tightrope traditions.
note: Naming source for the Acrobat class.

name: Kathputli
effect: Rajasthani string-puppet storytelling.
note: An idle animation set - cards moving as though on strings.

name: Ganjifa
effect: Mughal-era hand-painted circular playing cards; the Dashavatara version has ten suits.
note: A ten-suit deck makes flushes nearly impossible, which is a whole game of its own.

name: Vidushaka
effect: The Sanskrit-drama jester and Kerala's temple jester-narrator, licensed to mock anyone present.
note: Another entry in the fool's-licence family, from a different tradition.

name: Bed of Nails
effect: Ascetic endurance turned spectacle - fire walking and beds of nails recur across Greece, Fiji and India.
note: A card that takes weight without breaking, which the tall-stack family needs.

name: Uran Nugaralt
effect: Mongolian contortion, a national art with the world's most celebrated lineage - a card that fits into any cell shape a blind imposes.
note: The India-Rubber Man's better-sourced sibling.

name: Naadam
effect: The three manly games and a standing-gallop riding culture - a festival node with several contests.
note: A multi-contest event node.

name: Sema
effect: Sufi spinning meditation, frequently borrowed with varying respect by spectacle.
note: Visual reference, with the borrowing caveat attached.

name: Rifa'i Demonstrations
effect: Skewers and blades passed through flesh without visible harm - faith as proof.
note: A protection card whose flavour is conviction rather than equipment.

name: Moroccan Acrobats
effect: The Tazeroualt tumbling brotherhood, whose human pyramids and banquine throws toured the world.
note: The pyramid formation with a specific lineage.

name: The Gali-Gali Men
effect: Egyptian street cups-and-balls masters famed for producing live baby chicks - a card that creates a token wherever it moves.
note: Production rather than transformation.

name: Karagoz and Hacivat
effect: The Turkish shadow-play duo - the earthy trickster and the pompous scholar, bickering for five centuries. Two cards that score more when adjacent and argue when apart.
note: A pair whose whole value is the pairing.

name: Zurkhaneh
effect: The House of Strength - ritual club-swinging and drumming in an ancient athletic brotherhood.
note: The Strongman family, sourced to a living tradition.

name: Darvoz Rope-Walkers
effect: Central Asian high-rope dynasties performing at festivals for centuries.
note: A wire card that crosses between grids rather than within one.

name: Griots
effect: West African hereditary praise-singers and living archives - a card that remembers everything the run has done and scores for it.
note: Memory as a mechanic, and the only card that reads the whole run's history.

name: Gnawa
effect: Moroccan trance-music brotherhoods whose ceremonies include acrobatic dance.
note: Audio and visual reference, treated as sacred rather than as spectacle.

name: Egungun
effect: Yoruba ancestor masquerades, often on stilts, embodying returned spirits - sacred, not spectacle.
note: Recorded with its caveat: this is not a performance to mine casually.

name: Moko Jumbies
effect: Carnival stilt-walking guardians who see over evil - a card that sees and protects the whole column beneath it.
note: Guardianship with a height requirement.

name: Circus Ethiopia
effect: Youth circus as social work, spreading from Addis Ababa from 1991 onward.
note: The modern social-circus movement, and a different reason for a troupe to exist.

name: Danza de los Voladores
effect: Four flyers descend a thirty-metre pole on ropes, circling thirteen times each - a card that descends its stack scoring once per level.
note: Thirteen circles times four is the solar year, which is a meld waiting to be printed.

name: Aztec Antipodism
effect: Foot-jugglers spinning logs, documented in 1528 and taken to the court of Charles V - a card that supports and spins the card above it.
note: The Risley act's older name and better provenance.

name: Escaramuza
effect: Mexican women's precision team riding - several cards that move together in a fixed pattern and score for holding it.
note: Formation as choreography rather than as a static shape.

name: Carpas
effect: Mexican family tent-shows, where Cantinflas began - the small-tent starting deck.
note: A small deck with one grid and everything sharpened.

name: Circo Criollo
effect: Argentina's creole circus, mixing acrobatics with gaucho melodrama - circus as national theatre.
note: A deck whose cards tell one story as they score.

name: Rodeo Clown
effect: The clown whose real job is drawing the bull away from fallen riders - this card redirects a hazard onto itself.
note: The protection family's clearest single card.

name: Congress of Rough Riders
effect: Buffalo Bill's touring mega-show mixed cowboys, Cossacks and cavalry from everywhere - a card that scores for the number of distinct classes on the whole board.
note: The rainbow reward at board scale, and the historical original of the variety show.

name: Sitting Bull's Season
effect: The Lakota leader toured one season, charging for autographs and giving much of it away.
note: An event where a card joins for one show only and sets its own price. Handle the framing with care.

name: The Rattlesnake King
effect: Clark Stanley's snake oil, which contained no snake oil - a card sold at a shop whose printed effect is not its real one.
note: The medicine show, and the origin of a phrase.

name: Chautauqua
effect: Improving tent circuits of lectures, music and uplift - a node that grants no fame but permanently improves a card.
note: Teddy Roosevelt called them the most American thing in America.

name: Playing the Palace
effect: The Keith-Albee and Orpheum circuits, with the Palace as the summit every act was climbing toward.
note: The tour's final city, with a real name.

name: The Hook
effect: Amateur nights yanked bad acts offstage with a shepherd's crook - score too little in a refill and a card is pulled from the board.
note: A gentler Gong, applied to cards rather than to the show.

name: Wing Walkers
effect: Barnstormers and wing-walkers of the 1920s - a card that transfers between grids while both are in motion.
note: A mid-flight transfer, which is the most dangerous move in the file and should score like it.

name: Annie Edson Taylor
effect: A sixty-three-year-old teacher, first over Niagara in a barrel, who saw almost no money from it.
note: A card that survives an enormous risk and is paid almost nothing - which is worth printing honestly.

name: The Great Farini
effect: The Niagara rope-crosser who became an impresario and designed the human-cannonball apparatus.
note: A leader who builds the props other cards use.

name: Steve Brodie
effect: Claimed, probably falsely, to have jumped off the Brooklyn Bridge, and became famous anyway - a card that scores for a feat it never performs, unless it is inspected.
note: Fame from an unverified claim, which is the Gaff family's purest case.

name: High-Diving Horses
effect: The Steel Pier act, whose rider Sonora Webster continued after being blinded.
note: An Animal card that dives the full height of its stack.

name: Evel Knievel
effect: The declared-jump daredevil - announce the impossible, and the crash is part of the show.
note: The Booking's American cousin: the announcement is the product, whether or not you land it.

name: Luna Park
effect: Coney Island's electric dream-cities, of which Dreamland burned in 1911.
note: A city node that can be destroyed and rebuilt across a run.

name: The Incubator
effect: Dr Couney ran premature-infant incubators as a Coney Island sideshow for decades, saving thousands - a card that grows while enclosed and pays out when released.
note: An anti-spotlight card whose history is genuinely extraordinary.

name: Capoeira
effect: A martial art disguised as dance by enslaved Afro-Brazilians - the roda circle, the berimbau, and a fight the authorities could not see.
note: The ban-workaround family's founding card. Treat the history with weight.

name: Samba Schools
effect: Neighbourhood schools spend a whole year building one judged parade.
note: A meta-progression where the whole run prepares a single show.

name: Parintins
effect: Two ox-troupes, red Garantido and blue Caprichoso, battle across nights in a stadium split between them.
note: A two-faction level where each grid answers to a different judge.

name: Bumba Meu Boi
effect: The folk pageant beneath Parintins - the prize ox is killed and resurrected amid celebration.
note: A card that must die to pay out, and comes back.

name: Cordel
effect: Ballad-pamphlets hung on strings in north-eastern Brazilian markets, with cheap woodcut covers.
note: An art treatment and a shop layout in one - cards hung from a line.

name: Repentistas
effect: Improvised verse duelists trading stanzas until one falters.
note: The duel system's South American skin.

name: Danza de las Tijeras
effect: Peru's scissors dance, where competing danzaq trade increasingly acrobatic and dangerous feats.
note: Escalating one-upmanship - the duel system with a rising stake.

name: La Diablada
effect: Oruro's carnival devil-dance, where the archangel defeats the Seven Deadly Sins in fabulous masks.
note: A boss with seven named sub-effects, one per sin.

name: Diablos Danzantes
effect: Venezuelan red-masked devils dance through the town and then kneel in submission.
note: A hazard that ends by surrendering, which is a genuinely different arc.

name: Tango
effect: Born in dockside courtyards and brothels, then conquered Paris - the embrace, the lead and the follow.
note: Two cards that move as a pair, one leading and one following.

name: Frevo
effect: Carnival music so frenetic that dancers invented the passo - acrobatics steadied by a tiny umbrella.
note: A prop that permits a move otherwise illegal. The umbrella is the enabler.

name: Murga
effect: Whiteface carnival choirs satirising the year's news - the annual reckoning.
note: A level whose effects are drawn from what the run itself has done.

name: Fuerza Bruta
effect: Post-theatre spectacle - performers sprinting on treadmills through walls of the set.
note: A reference for what maximum kinetic presentation looks like.

name: Inti Raymi
effect: The restaged Inca Festival of the Sun, solstice pageantry at Sacsayhuaman.
note: A calendar event that only appears at a certain point in a run.

name: Ashton's Circus
effect: Australia's founding circus, from 1847, and one of the oldest continuously running family shows anywhere.
note: Lineage as meta-progression - a troupe that persists between runs.

name: May Wirth
effect: The Australian equestrienne called the greatest ever, and the only performer landing a backward-backward somersault between horses.
note: A movement card whose whole claim is that only one person ever did it.

name: Sharman's Boxing Tent
effect: Sixty years of the sideshow-alley cry - who will take a glove - with locals challenging the troupe.
note: The duel system's Australian skin, and the only one where the challenger is a stranger.

name: Sideshow Alley
effect: Australia's agricultural-show circuit of rides, showbags and dagwood dogs.
note: A node that sells bundles rather than single cards.

name: Circus Oz
effect: Collectivist, political and defiantly star-free - everyone rigs, everyone clowns, nobody headlines.
note: A deck with no leader card, where every card is equal and slightly better for it.

name: Gravity and Other Myths
effect: The Australian contemporary-acro wave - no apparatus, no glitter, just bodies.
note: An art direction for a stripped-back card set.

name: The Flying Fruit Fly Circus
effect: Australia's national youth circus, where children train as full performers.
note: A progression where cards start weak and are trained rather than bought.

name: Songlines
effect: Routes across the continent encoded as song - navigation, law and story in one form.
note: Recorded with care: this is sacred knowledge, not a map mechanic to lift.

name: Haka and Kapa Haka
effect: The challenge dance, performed at welcomes, funerals and tests, and the competitive group form.
note: A whole-line card performed in unison. Treat the reference respectfully.

name: Siva Afi
effect: The Samoan fire-knife dance - the ailao war dance armed with a machete wrapped in burning towels.
note: Knives and Flames in one card, which is the dual-suit idea with a real source.

name: Naghol
effect: Pentecost Island land diving - men dive from thirty-metre towers with vines tied to their ankles, calculated to stop just short.
note: The Vine stamp: survive a fall from any height, exactly once.

name: Sing-Sing
effect: Hundreds of clans gather to share dance, music and bodypaint at once.
note: An event that grants one card of every class you do not yet own.

name: Hula and the Halau
effect: Story told through the body, taught in schools under a kumu who keeps the lineage of each dance.
note: A deck whose cards must be learned in order.

name: Tangata Manu
effect: The Rapa Nui birdman race - swim to an islet and retrieve the season's first egg.
note: A race event where the first objective completed wins and the rest score nothing.

name: Namsadang
effect: Korean itinerant commoner troupes, social outcasts performing six arts at once.
note: A six-class deck where no class may be dropped.

name: Jultagi
effect: Korean tightrope walking with stand-up comedy - the walker jokes mid-wire and works the crowd.
note: An Acrobat card that is also a Clown card, and better for it.

name: Talchum
effect: Korean masked satire mocking aristocrats and monks, with licence to insult the powerful.
note: Another fool's-licence card, from a tradition where the licence was explicit.

name: Sangmo
effect: Pungmul drummers spinning long ribbons from swivel-hats while drumming and leaping.
note: A prop that traces a path over several cells while its card stays put.

name: The Dalang
effect: One person voices every character in an all-night shadow epic, and runs the orchestra too.
note: A card that operates every other card in its grid for one refill.

name: Reog Ponorogo
effect: A dancer carries a fifty-kilogram lion-peacock mask gripped in his teeth.
note: The Iron Jaw card with the heaviest documented load.

name: Kuda Lumping
effect: Javanese trance horse-dancers on woven bamboo horses, who in trance eat glass.
note: A status that grants immunity and costs control.

name: Barong and Rangda
effect: The eternal Balinese battle between protective lion-spirit and witch, in which neither ever wins.
note: The Balance boss - equalise the row and column terms instead of maximising either.

name: Kecak
effect: The monkey chant - a hundred bare-chested men as a single interlocking voice-orchestra, devised in the 1930s.
note: A line where every card contributes one interlocking part and none scores alone.

name: Water Puppetry
effect: Vietnamese puppets dance on a pond while the puppeteers stand waist-deep behind a screen.
note: Hidden but active - the anti-spotlight family with the prettiest staging.

name: Yoke The
effect: Burmese marionette theatre so prestigious that puppets outranked human actors.
note: A hierarchy where the token outranks the card that made it.

name: Likay
effect: Glitter-drenched improvised Thai folk theatre, where audiences pin money on performers mid-scene.
note: Tips arriving during the act rather than after it.

name: Khon
effect: The masked dance-drama of the Ramakien, with codified roles - hero, demon, monkey.
note: Three named roles that map cleanly onto card archetypes.

name: Balagtasan
effect: Staged Filipino poetic debates, named for the poet Balagtas - verse duels as public entertainment.
note: The duel system's Philippine skin.

name: Perya and Higantes
effect: Travelling fairs with colour-wheel games, and Angono's festival of giants.
note: A node built around a wheel of fortune, and a parade of enormous cards.

name: Wau Bulan
effect: Malaysian giant moon-kites with hummers that sing in the wind.
note: A prop that stays aloft over a column and hums until it lands.

name: Sbek Thom
effect: Cambodian sacred shadow-panels - whole scenes carved from a single hide and danced before a fire.
note: One image containing a whole scene, which is what the effect pop-up wants to be.

name: Phare Ponleu Selpak
effect: The circus school born in a refugee-camp drawing class, now Battambang's company.
note: Social circus as a run's framing, and the most hopeful entry in the file.

name: Canboulay
effect: Trinidad's carnival was born from emancipation celebrations, and the 1881 riots followed attempts to suppress it.
note: A ban level that the player breaks rather than endures.

name: Extempo
effect: Calypso's crowned annual champion, and improvised lyrical duels on stage.
note: The duel system's Trinidadian skin.

name: Steelpan
effect: When drums were banned, Trinidadians hammered melody out of oil barrels and invented an instrument.
note: The ban-workaround family's best outcome - a restriction that produces something new.

name: Moko Jumbies cross-reference
effect: The stilt guardians are catalogued under Africa and cross-referenced here.
note: A pointer row, kept so the cross-reference resolves.

name: J'ouvert
effect: The pre-dawn opening of carnival - mud, oil and paint. Get dirty before you get glorious.
note: An event that debuffs every card and pays for it later.

name: Dubplate
effect: Jamaican sound systems battle for crowds, and the ammunition is the dubplate - an exclusive cut nobody else has.
note: A card that exists in one copy in one run, and is worth more for it.

name: Rara
effect: Haitian Lenten street processions with bamboo vaksin trumpets - bands walk for miles gathering crowds.
note: A card that collects other cards as it travels a row.

name: The Tropicana
effect: Havana's open-air cabaret, paradise under the stars, from 1939.
note: The cabaret city - a node where presentation scores more than power.

name: Dia de los Muertos
effect: The dead honoured with ofrendas, marigolds and calaveras - festive remembrance rather than mourning.
note: An event that brings back a card removed earlier in the run.

name: Guelaguetza
effect: The Oaxacan festival of reciprocal gift-giving, where regions exchange dances and goods.
note: An event where giving a card away returns a better one.

name: Castells
effect: Catalan human towers up to ten levels, crowned by the enxaneta - a small child who climbs to the very top and raises a hand.
note: The crown rule is the mechanic: the smallest card must top the tower for it to count.

name: Las Fallas
effect: Valencian neighbourhoods spend a year building enormous satirical sculptures and then burn every one, except a single pardoned ninot.
note: Build-to-burn, with one survivor chosen by vote. Investment that pays out on destruction.

name: Recortadores
effect: Spanish bull-leaping - dodging and vaulting the bull with no harm done to it.
note: The Minoan act, still performed, and the humane version of the Bullfight card.

name: Duende
effect: The untranslatable state when a performance stops being technique and becomes possession.
note: A card that scores enormously but only once per run, when the conditions happen to align.

name: The Costaleros
effect: Monumental Holy Week floats carried through cities by hidden bearers sweating underneath.
note: Covered cards add their rank to the card they carry - the anti-spotlight family's best mechanic.

name: Fado
effect: Portuguese song as performed longing - mourning what is gone, as public art.
note: A card that scores for what the run has lost rather than for what it holds.

name: Flyting
effect: Norse skalds whose praise made reputations, and the formal exchange of insults that could unmake them.
note: The duel system's Norse skin, and the oldest documented one.

name: Glima
effect: Icelandic belt-wrestling, still practised - codified, courteous and ancient.
note: A friendly duel that costs nothing to lose.

name: Czech Marionettes
effect: Under occupation, puppets kept the Czech language and its satire alive when people could not speak.
note: The ban-workaround family, again, and its most literal case.

name: Vertep
effect: Portable nativity puppet-theatres - a whole stage carried in a box.
note: A grid that folds up and travels with you between shows.

name: The Puszta Five
effect: Hungarian csikos standing astride five galloping horses at once.
note: One card belonging to all five columns simultaneously, which is the boldest geometry in the file.

name: Hopak
effect: The Ukrainian squat-kick acrobatic dance - explosive, competitive and showy.
note: A burst move that launches a card upward one level.

name: Fasnacht
effect: Basel's masked pre-dawn carnival - piccolos, drums and lantern floats satirising the year.
note: Another annual-reckoning event, drawing on the run's own history.

name: The Bauta
effect: The Venetian mask that let all classes mingle anonymously - nobles gambled beside servants.
note: A stamp that hides a card's rarity, which several blinds care about.

name: Romani Performers
effect: Centuries of virtuoso musicianship, horse expertise and fairground craft, carried across a Europe that persecuted them.
note: Recorded with its caveat: credit the craft, never the caricature.

name: Gumboot Dance
effect: South African miners forbidden to speak invented a slap-and-stamp boot code.
note: A card that communicates with others in its line while an effect silences them.

name: Azmari
effect: Ethiopian wandering minstrels famed for wax and gold - lyrics with a surface meaning and a hidden one.
note: A card whose printed text says one thing and whose real effect is the other.

name: Sogo Bo
effect: Malian puppet-masquerade festivals of animal spirits on the Niger - whole ecosystems danced.
note: A card that spawns a set of Animal tokens that interact with each other.

name: Tahtib
effect: Egyptian stick-fighting as game-dance, millennia old and shown on pharaonic reliefs.
note: The duel system's oldest documented skin.

name: Tanoura
effect: The secular Egyptian spinning dance, rainbow skirts blooming into discs of colour.
note: A spin animation that reads as a bloom rather than as a rotation.

name: Katajjaq
effect: Inuit throat-singing games - two women face to face trading rhythmic patterns until one laughs.
note: The duel system where losing means laughing, which is the friendliest version of it.

name: Ajaraaq
effect: Inuit string figures - story-patterns woven between the hands.
note: A card that scores for the shape the board makes rather than for its values.

name: Greenlandic Drum Duels
effect: Disputes settled by song duel, with the community laughing the loser into submission.
note: The duel system as a justice mechanism, which is a genuinely different framing.

name: Disciplines index
effect: Part B sorts the same material by discipline rather than by region - aerial and wire, juggling, strength, danger acts and clowning.
note: The second index into the same quarry.

name: Flyer and Catcher
effect: The trapeze duet - one throws, one catches, and trust is the art form.
note: Two cards where one launches and the other must be in position to receive.

name: Iron Jaw and Hair Hang
effect: Aerialists suspended by their teeth, or by braided hair in the Chinese tradition.
note: Two support cards from one act, differing in what they can carry.

name: The Aerial Family
effect: Cloud swing, corde lisse, Spanish web and silks - the rope-and-fabric family.
note: Four movement cards distinguished by how far and how controllably they descend.

name: Philippe Petit
effect: The illegal 1974 wire-walk between the Twin Towers, prepared in secret for years.
note: A cross-grid walk that must be set up over several refills before it can be taken.

name: Karl Wallenda
effect: The patriarch who walked until seventy-three and died on the wire - being on the wire is life, the rest is waiting.
note: A leader who cannot stop performing, and is penalised for a refill spent idle.

name: Maria Spelterini
effect: Crossed Niagara on a wire in 1876 with peach baskets strapped to her feet.
note: A movement card with a self-imposed handicap that multiplies the payout.

name: Enrico Rastelli
effect: The god of jugglers, who trained obsessively and died at thirty-four, and whose records are still argued about.
note: The Balls-suit leader, whose signature is sheer count.

name: Paul Cinquevalli
effect: The Victorian greatest juggler - billiard balls and everyday objects handled with elegance.
note: A card that treats any adjacent card as a prop it can juggle.

name: Gentleman Jugglers
effect: Kara and the immaculate evening-dress school - hats, canes and cigars, the everyday made impossible.
note: Props drawn from ordinary cards rather than from the suit.

name: W C Fields
effect: The vaudeville tramp juggler whose fake mistakes got bigger laughs than his tricks.
note: The Deliberate Wobble card's American source.

name: Kris Kremo
effect: Cigar-box virtuosity - three boxes and decades of variations.
note: Rearrange three cards in a stack in a single action.

name: Michael Moschen
effect: Contact juggling and crystal balls - his hands played Bowie's in Labyrinth.
note: The visual reference for a prop that never leaves the performer's hands.

name: Club Passing
effect: Jugglers exchanging clubs in a shared pattern - two Juggler cards in different grids trading props between them.
note: The cross-grid prop exchange, and a strong argument for playing several grids at once.

name: The Manipulation Family
effect: Devil sticks, poi and staff - the object-manipulation family across cultures, poi from Maori tradition.
note: Three common prop cards, with the poi entry carrying its provenance.

name: Thomas Topham
effect: London's first celebrity strongman, who lifted three hogsheads of water.
note: A naming source for the Strongman tier.

name: Louis Cyr's Backlift
effect: The Canadian who back-lifted a platform of eighteen men - this card scores for every card resting above it.
note: The purest anti-spotlight card: it wants to be buried under as much as possible.

name: Eugen Sandow
effect: The father of bodybuilding, and Ziegfeld's realisation that crowds paid to look rather than to see lifting.
note: The presentation-over-substance insight, from the man it made famous.

name: Katie Sandwina
effect: Bent iron bars and lifted her husband overhead nightly for decades - carries one card without it counting as covering.
note: Support that does not block the spotlight.

name: The Mighty Atom
effect: A five-foot-four strongman who bit through nails, restrained aircraft and broke chains with his chest.
note: A low-rank card that behaves as a high one for every strength check.

name: Zishe Breitbart
effect: The Jewish strongman folk hero of the 1920s, billed as the modern Samson.
note: A folk-hero naming source.

name: The Hunger Artist
effect: Professional public fasters in barred cages, and Kafka's story about the last of them - a card that grows stronger the longer it stays undrawn.
note: The deck-position family's most literary entry.

name: Flagpole Sitter
effect: Weeks-long endurance perching above city crowds - a card that scores for every refill it remains the top of its stack.
note: Payment for doing nothing, provided nobody displaces you.

name: Dance Marathons
effect: Depression-era endurance contests where couples shuffled for weeks for prize money.
note: The Marathon blind's source, including the grimness.

name: Pedestrianism
effect: Competitive long-distance walking, the biggest spectator sport of the 1870s.
note: A multi-node objective completed across several shows.

name: Hadji Ali
effect: The regurgitation act - swallowed water and kerosene and fountained them separately, extinguishing and reigniting a fire.
note: A card that stores two effects and releases them in either order.

name: The Target Girl
effect: Knife and axe throwing around a human assistant - the thrower gets billing and the target takes the risk.
note: A card that stands in for another as the destination of every knife prop.

name: The Wheel of Death
effect: An assistant spinning on a disc while blades land around her.
note: A rotating grid, where the whole board turns one step per refill.

name: The Mirror Shot
effect: Sharpshooters firing over the shoulder using a mirror, as Oakley and Topperwein did.
note: A card that targets by reflection - the cell mirrored across the grid's centre.

name: Bullet catch cross-reference
effect: The bullet catch is specced in the recommendations and cross-referenced here.
note: A pointer row.

name: Buried Alive reference
effect: The fakir tradition and Houdini's last stunts - interment endurance, which Houdini nearly died failing.
note: The Buried Alive card's source, with the failure included.

name: The Escape Chain
effect: The Water Torture Cell - upside down, ankles locked, and a series of restraints that must be undone in order.
note: Several restrictions removed one per refill, which is a quest inside one card.

name: Fire Acts
effect: Fire eating, fire breathing and full-body burns - vaporised-fuel plumes and stunt burns, the least forgiving discipline there is.
note: The Flames suit's most dangerous tier.

name: Edith Clifford
effect: Swallowed a bayonet mounted on a rifle butt while the band played.
note: The Sword Swallower card's specific and astonishing source.

name: The Globe of Death
effect: Motorcyclists riding vertical walls and mesh spheres - a card that circles its column continuously without leaving it.
note: Centrifugal movement, which is a loop rather than a path.

name: Zazel
effect: The first human cannonball, 1877, and the Zacchini family who made it a dynasty with compressed air and faked smoke.
note: The Human Cannonball card's source, including the fact that the explosion was theatre.

name: Human Blockhead
effect: Melvin Burkhart hammering a nail into his nasal cavity, with comedy timing rather than gore.
note: A cheap card whose delivery is the whole act.

name: The Lion's Bride
effect: The caged-beauty tableaus of the menagerie era, and snake-handling acts alongside them.
